stages.name: The Lewis model
stages.title: The Lewis model
stages.sub: Trace how the Lewis model explains growth through structural change, and judge its strengths and weaknesses.

steps.q: Workers have moved from low-paid farm work into city factories, earning wages for the factory owner. If the owner keeps the profit, what would growing the business further require?
steps.right: Putting the profit back into more machines and factories
steps.wrong: Giving the profit straight to the farm workers left behind
steps.hint: Think about what a factory owner does with profit if they want to produce even more next year.

steps.q: Each year, more capital means more jobs pulling workers off the land. Can this carry on forever if the countryside only has a limited number of spare workers?
steps.right: No, eventually there is no spare farm labour left to pull in
steps.wrong: Yes, it can carry on without ever slowing
steps.hint: The farm workforce is not infinite. What happens once the spare workers have all moved?
steps.pre: So the process runs until the surplus farm labour runs out, transforming the economy's structure. That is

steps.q: A country moves from mostly subsistence farming to a growing industrial base, with output and wages both rising over time. Does this story give a plausible explanation of how developing economies can grow?
steps.right: Yes, it plausibly explains industrial growth
steps.wrong: No, it explains nothing about growth
steps.hint: Think about whether the step-by-step shift from farm to factory is a believable route to a bigger economy.

steps.q: Suppose the factory owner instead sends the profits abroad or spends them on luxury goods rather than new machines. Would the second step of the model, reinvestment building more capital, still happen?
steps.right: No, the model's growth process would break down
steps.wrong: Yes, growth would carry on exactly as before
steps.hint: Step 2 depends on profits going back into the business. What if they don't?

steps.q: The model assumes farms always have endless spare workers ready to move, and that every worker who moves to the city instantly finds a factory job. If population growth changes the number of spare workers, or cities actually have high unemployment, does the model's picture still match reality?
steps.right: No, its assumptions may not hold in practice
steps.wrong: Yes, the assumptions always hold regardless
steps.hint: Think about whether unlimited surplus labour and instant urban jobs are realistic, especially once demographic factors are considered.
